  is small, we can therefore compute n rapidly by nding the digits from right to left in
  its mixed-radix representation, for radices q1 , : : : , qt . (This idea is due to R. L. Silver,
  1975; see S. C. Pohlig and M. Hellman, IEEE Transactions IT-24 (1978), 106{110.)
       John M. Pollard discovered an elegant way to compute discrete logs with about
  O(pp ) operations mod p, requiring very little memory, based on the theory of random
  mappings. See Math. Comp. 32 (1978), 918{924, where he also suggests another
  method based on numbers nj = rj mod p that have only small prime factors.
       Asymptotically faster methods are discussed in exercise 4.5.4{39.
